concepts.concept: Constructing a graph from a Set<T> of keys, and the AL vs AM representation tradeoff

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — computer part
futureAppearances.description: The Final's coding section asks you to extend an abstract Graph<T> in both AdjacencyList and AdjacencyMatrix forms — the same constructor + representation-choice work you did in Milestone 1, but with a fresh method on top.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Paper-section questions ask you to pick AL vs AM for a given workload and justify the choice in big-O terms — the same reasoning the testRelativeSpeed tests pin down empirically.

concepts.concept: Adding directed edges with vertex preconditions and the boolean already-present return

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — computer part
futureAppearances.description: Every graph drill on the Final starts by building a small graph via addEdge calls. If addEdge silently accepts edges into missing vertices, all downstream traversal questions read wrong answers.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Paper tracing questions step through addEdge calls one at a time, asking you to report the resulting adjacency list or matrix. Confidence with the boolean and exception contract makes those questions fast.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Reachability and edge-existence questions on the paper section depend on the same membership semantics hasEdge enforces: a directed edge (from,to) exists iff to is in from's successor set.

futureAppearances.label: java.util.Set contract
futureAppearances.description: keySet() returns the backing Set of vertex keys. Re-reading the Set interface clarifies what equality semantics callers may rely on — the same contract recurs in EditorTrees iteration and any future Set-returning method.

concepts.concept: Computing in-degree and out-degree of a vertex

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Degree-sequence reasoning shows up in paper-section questions about Eulerian paths, balanced graphs, and edge counting (sum of out-degrees = numEdges).

concepts.concept: Returning the neighbor set of a vertex (successors / predecessors)

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: BFS and DFS trace tables on the paper section list the successor set of each visited vertex at every step. The same Set-returning method is the building block for both algorithms.

futureAppearances.label: java.util.Set contract
futureAppearances.description: predecessorSet and successorSet must return a defensive-or-snapshot Set, not a live view. Reviewing the Set contract clarifies the iteration / mutation guarantees your callers expect.

concepts.concept: Lazy iterators over a vertex's neighbors (constructor and first next() must be O(1) amortized)

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — computer part
futureAppearances.description: The Final's graph problem traverses the graph via successorIterator inside an inner loop — if your iterator is non-lazy (eagerly building a Set on construction), the perf-bound test that follows the correctness test will time out.

futureAppearances.label: java.util.Iterator contract
futureAppearances.description: Every iterator you write — graphs, hash sets, EditorTrees — satisfies the same hasNext()/next()/NoSuchElementException contract. Re-reading the docs after a failing iterator test usually surfaces the rule that was violated.

concepts.concept: Removing edges while keeping numEdges and adjacency state in sync

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing — Milestone 1 spec recap
futureAppearances.description: The Milestone 1 section of the spec restates the removeEdge contract: returns true if the remove succeeds, false if the edge wasn't present, NoSuchElementException for missing endpoints. Re-reading it is a fast way to sanity-check edge cases the unit tests check.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Mutate-the-graph trace questions sequence addEdge and removeEdge calls and ask you to report numEdges after each step. The same invariant your tests check — numEdges decreases by exactly 1 per successful remove — is the answer key.

concepts.concept: BFS shortest path on a directed graph (List<T> from start to end, or empty if unreachable)

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — computer part
futureAppearances.description: Shortest path is the canonical Final graph-programming question: implement a method that returns a List of vertices from start to end, or an empty list if no path exists. Same signature, same BFS-with-parent-map approach as Milestone 2.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Paper questions ask you to trace BFS on a small graph and report the parent-of array at each step. The same bookkeeping that recovers the path in shortestPath is what the trace table is testing.

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing — Milestone 2 spec recap
futureAppearances.description: The Milestone 2 section of the spec describes shortestPath's exact contract — start/end inclusion in the returned list, empty-list-on-unreachable, NoSuchElementException for missing keys. Re-read before practicing for the Final to make sure your mental model matches the contract.

futureAppearances.label: java.util.List contract
futureAppearances.description: shortestPath returns a List<T>. The List interface specifies ordering, indexed access, and equality semantics — re-reading it clarifies why an ArrayList works and a HashSet would not.

concepts.concept: Strongly connected component of a vertex (forward and reverse reachability intersection)

futureAppearances.label: Final 2023 — findUnknownBalloons
futureAppearances.description: The 2023 Final's graph question asks you to find balloons not in any confirmed network — i.e., not in the same SCC as any confirmed balloon. Solving it is a thin layer over your Milestone 2 stronglyConnectedComponent, and matches the standard Final-Exam pattern of building one new question on top of an M1/M2 method.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — computer part
futureAppearances.description: SCC, cycle counting, and reachability-based methods are common Final graph-section questions. The two-pass forward/reverse-BFS approach you used for stronglyConnectedComponent generalizes directly to those problems.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — paper section
futureAppearances.description: Paper questions ask you to identify the SCCs of a small directed graph by inspection. Practicing this by hand is faster than re-tracing your code and is the form the Final usually uses.

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing — Milestone 2 spec recap
futureAppearances.description: The Milestone 2 section explains why SCC matters (defining a 'universe' of mutually-reachable wiki pages) — the conceptual framing the Final's SCC question will assume you understand.

concepts.concept: Integrating shortestPath and SCC against a real 460k-vertex graph (WikiSurfing)

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing — Milestone 2 spec recap
futureAppearances.description: The WikiSurfing section describes the Living-People graph, the data origin, and the bonus challenge-pair task. WikiSurfing failures usually trace back to a Milestone 1 method that's correct on tiny examples but quadratic on a large graph — re-reading the spec helps locate which method is the bottleneck.

futureAppearances.label: Final practice — computer part
futureAppearances.description: The Final's graph question is graded for O(N+E) traversal on a moderately-sized random graph. The same performance discipline that lets your shortestPath finish a Living-People query in seconds is what the Final's perf test asserts.
